query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The stability of near‐equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles at high temperatures (773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectrics) is governed by an intrinsic, entropy‐driven lattice distortion that creates high diffusion barriers. This sluggish atomic mobility prevents phase segregation and elemental coalescence despite thermal activation, thereby preserving both the single-phase structure and the uniform chemical distribution even in catalytic environments with low noble-metal content.
generation.material_initial_state: Rapidly synthesized, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles (e.g., Ru‐5 MEA‐NPs or similar HEA nanoparticles) with a homogeneous distribution of elements and pronounced lattice distortions due to multi‐element mixing.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one as a high‐entropy, near‐equiatomic solid solution to maximize lattice distortion and a comparable binary or low‐complexity alloy (with similar noble metal content) but with minimal lattice distortion. Both should be synthesized under otherwise identical high‐temperature and rapid quench conditions.
generation.conditions: Service conditions include prolonged exposure to high temperatures (773–1173 K for catalytic operation and up to 1923 K for thermoelectric applications) under inert or controlled atmospheres to avoid extrinsic oxidation effects. Measurements should be made before and after thermal aging/annealing.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of lattice distortion and the resulting activation energy for atomic diffusion serve as key mediators. In high-entropy nanoparticles, the configurational entropy creates a distorted lattice that slows self-diffusion compared to binary alloys.
generation.mechanism: Multi-element mixing yields a high configurational entropy that stabilizes a single-phase structure not merely on thermodynamic grounds, but also by kinetically hindering atomic diffusion. Enhanced lattice distortions increase activation barriers for atom migration, thus preventing elemental segregation and sintering during high-temperature operation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical thermal treatments, high-entropy nanoparticles will show minimal changes in lattice spacing and elemental distribution (confirmed by diffraction and compositional mapping), whereas the binary (or low-complexity) alloy control will display evidence of phase segregation, coarsening, or elemental clustering. Consequently, the catalytic and thermoelectric performance of the high-entropy nanoparticles will remain stable relative to a degradation observed in the control sample.
generation.baseline: Binary or low-complexity alloy nanoparticles with similar average composition but reduced configurational entropy and lattice distortion will rapidly exhibit increased atomic diffusion, leading to phase separation and loss of uniform catalytic sites under the same thermal treatments.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for nanoparticles synthesized via rapid, high-temperature routes that effectively 'freeze in' the disordered solid-solution state, and for systems where the operating temperatures do not induce significant metal evaporation or support-related sintering effects. It may not apply if the nanoparticles are too large (where bulk diffusion dominates) or if compositional differences drive strong chemical ordering independent of diffusion kinetics.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis combines the evidence of entropy-induced sluggish diffusion and structural stability from PMC7069714 (entropy-driven simulation and diffusion studies in MEA-NPs) with the in situ thermal stability observations of Pt nanoparticles on carbon supports from PMC7733500. The new aspect is extending these insights to predict that the same fundamental mechanism governs long-term structural and chemical integrity in catalytic and thermoelectric service regimes; however, the precise threshold of lattice distortion needed remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: one using a method that maximizes high-entropy mixing (resulting in pronounced lattice distortions) and a control binary or low-complexity system with similar elemental amounts but minimal lattice distortion. Subject both to prolonged annealing at 773–1173 K. Characterize structural and chemical changes using in situ TEM, XRD, and elemental mapping (e.g., EDS).
measurements: Change in lattice parameters and peak broadening in XRD before and after annealing.
Elemental distribution homogeneity and evidence of phase segregation via TEM/EDS mapping.
Diffusion indicators (e.g., changes in particle size or coalescence) monitored by in situ heating TEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy nanoparticles exhibit similar degrees of phase segregation, coarsening, or elemental clustering as observed in the binary or low-complexity control after annealing, or if measures of lattice distortion do not correlate with suppressed diffusion, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion (driven by configurational entropy) governs the high-temperature stability would be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: The dispersion stability of the MEA-NPs can be explained by the following two reasons. First, we used high temperatures for the MEA-NP synthesis, and as a result, they naturally have high thermal stability. Second, the defects of the carbon nanofibers help to anchor these MEA-NPs onto the substrate with improved thermal stability. In terms of the observed structural stability, we believe that it originates from the entropy stabilization effect. Thermodynamically, multi-elemental mixing increases the mixing of entropy and favors an alloy structure. Kinetically, the mixing among different elements also leads to increased lattice distortion (table S3 for Ru MEA-NPs) and, therefore, sluggish diffusion, which prevents phase separation and elemental segregation (, ). To further verify the structural stability, we performed MD simulations to calculate the self-diffusion coefficient of the Ru element in Ru-5 MEA and compared it with Ru in a binary Ru-Ni alloy. We found that the Ru atoms in the Ru-Ni alloy diffuse about two orders of magnitude (100×) faster than in Ru-5 MEA (Fig. 4C), indicating that the sluggish diffusion in the MEA-NPs is due to the multi-elemental mixing and the resultan

We also simulated the overall diffusion in the MEA-NP using a hybrid MC + MD simulation approach, in which the MC swaps were attempted at a constant frequency during the MD simulation to model the annealing conditions at 773 K. The entropy-stabilized structure has less atom diffusion due to high diffusion barriers and sluggish kinetics, resulting in uniform elemental distribution after annealing. Figure 4D shows the statistical probability of the nearest composition distributions for each element in Ru-5 MEA-NPs, displaying its microscopic/atomic arrangement of different elements. We found the nearest-neighbor sites of each element equal to its nominal composition with only short-range fluctuations. As a comparison, when it is fully diffusion equilibrated, clear elemental segregation, especially for Ru, Rh, and Ni, is observed (fig. S5A), indicating that the entropy-induced slow kinetics are the key to stabilize the structure for thermal annealing. Similar entropy-stabilization results were also found when there is an extension of MC + MD’s time scale to 50 ns (fig. S5B) and in the Ru-4 MEA-NPs (fig. S5, C and D). cited_evidence.text: The MD simulations indicates that the nanoparticles are quite stable on the edge planes of T-graphite even at extremely high temperatures. To further verify the thermal stability of such nanoparticles, we performed in situ TEM heating on the CNFs decorated with Pt nanoparticles that were synthesized through ex situ Joule heating method. The ex situ formed nanoparticles appear to have very similar morphology to the in situ observations reported in this work. As it can be seen in Fig. 7a, the ultra-fine nanoparticles are located at wrinkled edge planes showing FCC structure (inset of Fig. 7a). The Pt-decorated CNFs are evaluated at various temperatures (573 K, 773 K, 973 K, and 1173 K). As shown in the high angle annular dark field (HAADF)-STEM image in Fig. 7b, the ultra-small Pt nanoparticles are well dispersed on CNF at room temperature (RT). High temperatures are expected to be detrimental to the nanoclusters’ stability, since the nanoparticles would fuse into larger particles to reduce the surface energy at elevated temperatures.
